title: What's the deal with totem poles?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a plug for a Science Channel pumpkin chunking TV special, then discuss totem poles: the myth of the "low man on the totem pole" (the lowest carvings are the most prominent, carved by the head carver), the history of totem poles (Hida tribe of southeastern Alaska as early carvers, boom after European contact, Captain James Cook's comment), what makes a pole authentic (trained Pacific Northwest carver, traditional ceremony, blessing, red or yellow cedar, no power tools, traditional colors, single piece of wood), lifespan of about a hundred years, types of poles (entryway, mortuary, shame poles), the Lincoln Pole in Alaska, potlatch celebrations, the decline in the twentieth century (potlatch bans, lost knowledge, theft by museums) and revival after the Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, costs of commissioned poles, record tallest and thickest poles (including the Victoria, British Columbia pole that was torn down), and a listener mail about listening to episodes out of order and an idea for a podcast on odd personal habits.
topics: low man on the totem pole

segments.title: Opening banter and pumpkin chunking plug
segments.summary: Hosts open the show, plug a Science Channel special on Delaware pumpkin chunking, and joke about the low man on the totem pole phrase.
topics: low man on the totem pole

segments.title: Low man on the totem pole and social rank
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the lowest carvings on a totem pole are the most prominent and were carved by the head carver, and that Native societies had social strata. Wealthy patrons commissioned head carvers, who were treated like royalty.
topics: low man on the totem pole

segments.title: Origins and history of totem poles
segments.summary: Totem poles are a relatively recent tradition. The Hida tribe of southeastern Alaska are thought to be the first carvers, and production boomed after European settlers arrived in the late 1700s. Captain James Cook called them monstrous figures.

segments.title: What makes a totem pole authentic
segments.summary: Authentic poles need a trained Pacific Northwest carver, traditional ceremony and blessing by local natives, red or yellow cedar, traditional colors, no power tools, and a single piece of wood. An authentic pole lasts about a hundred years.

segments.title: Types of poles and their figures
segments.summary: Poles commemorate events and carry figures such as eagles, thunderbirds, bears, owls, wolves, ravens, and frogs, each with cultural meaning. Pole types include entryway poles, mortuary poles that hold ashes, and shame poles.

segments.title: Lincoln Pole in Sitka
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Lincoln Pole in Sitka, Alaska, which was raised to shame the US government over the Emancipation Proclamation after Native slaves were freed.

segments.title: Potlatch, decline, and revival
segments.summary: Raising a pole is marked by a potlatch party. Canadian bans on potlatches, loss of carving traditions, and widespread theft by museums and collectors led to decline in the twentieth century. The NAGPRA law under President George H. W. Bush led to returns and renewed carving.
topics: Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act

segments.title: Cost of commissioned totem poles
segments.summary: The hosts estimate that an authentic commissioned pole costs roughly ten thousand to a hundred thousand dollars, while non-authentic poles are much cheaper.

segments.title: Record tallest and thickest totem poles
segments.summary: A British Columbia pole was claimed as the tallest, and a Guinness-certified 185-foot pole in Victoria, British Columbia was later torn down by an angry mob after controversy. The thickest pole, carved by Richard Hunt in British Columbia, has a six-foot diameter.

segments.title: Listener mail on listening out of order and odd habits
segments.summary: A listener writes that he hears episodes in reverse order on his iPod and suggests a podcast about people's odd personal habits. The hosts also give the contact address and point to the website.
